# Congo African Grey Parrot

The Congo African Grey is a medium-sized, highly observant African parrot, recognised by its scalloped grey plumage, pale face and bright red tail. Its remarkable ability to learn sounds is only one part of a complex, long-term relationship.

Scientific namePsittacus erithacus

Typical adult sizeAbout 33 cm long; approximately 400–550 g, with individual variation.

Lifetime planningOften several decades in captivity; plan for a long-term commitment rather than relying on a maximum-age figure.

## Overview and appearance

The Congo African Grey is the larger and paler of the two commonly recognised African grey forms. It has a charcoal-grey bill, pale facial skin, finely edged grey body feathers and a vivid red tail. Juvenile birds may have darker eyes that change as they mature. Appearance can help identify the form, but an individual bird’s history and identity should be confirmed independently when relevant.

In the wild this species is native to equatorial Africa, where it forages and travels in social groups. A companion bird retains strong sensory, social and exploratory needs; it is not simply a talking ornament.

## Temperament and social life

African Greys are often attentive and cautious observers. Many take time to feel secure with new people, objects or routines, and confidence varies substantially between individuals. Respecting body language and allowing choice helps build a more trusting relationship than expecting instant handling or affection.

A bird may form a close bond with one person, but should still learn to occupy itself and interact calmly with other household members. A predictable daily rhythm can be reassuring; sudden changes, prolonged isolation or pressure to interact may be difficult for some birds.

## Typical adult size

An adult Congo is roughly 33 cm from beak to tail and commonly weighs around 400–550 g. These are planning ranges, not standards for assessing an individual bird; sex, build and condition affect weight. A suitably sized enclosure needs room for fully extended wings, climbing and movement, not merely enough floor space to perch.

## Expected lifespan and long-term care

Published lifespan figures differ, but companion African Greys may live for several decades. Consider future housing, care costs and a trusted contingency caregiver before making a commitment.

## Talking and vocalisation

This species is celebrated for vocal mimicry and may learn words, household sounds or whistles. No bird is guaranteed to speak, use words meaningfully or stay quiet. Calls can be sharp and carry through a home, so consider neighbours and the normal sound level of daily life.

## Intelligence and reward-based training

Greys are quick to investigate patterns and benefit from short, positive-reinforcement sessions. Teach voluntary step-up, stationing, recall in safe spaces and comfortable movement into a carrier at the bird’s pace. Foraging puzzles and learning new behaviours provide mental work; avoid punishment, which can undermine trust.

## Diet and nutrition

Build a balanced, species-appropriate diet around a suitable formulated food and varied fresh vegetables, with fruit and other treats offered thoughtfully. Do not assume a seed-only mix is complete or copy a rigid online recipe. An avian veterinarian can advise on an individual plan, transitions and monitoring body condition; avoid routine supplements without professional advice.

## Housing, exercise and enrichment

Provide a sturdy enclosure with varied, safe perches, room to climb and flap, and supervised time in a bird-safe area. Rotate shreddable materials, foraging opportunities and toys, checking them regularly for damage. Daily attention should include independent play as well as interaction.

## Who may suit this species?

A Congo Grey may suit an experienced or carefully prepared household able to offer patience, routine, daily mental activity and a long-term plan. It is not automatically a beginner bird because it is famous for speech. Families should teach children calm observation and adult-supervised boundaries; the parrot must always have a quiet retreat.

Before enquiring, ask about the individual bird’s age, established diet, handling preferences, routine and current availability. Confirm what ongoing support is offered, how a bird travels to its new home and whether your household can accommodate noise, moult, cleaning and changing needs. Individual species stock needs confirmation; a species page is not an availability promise.
